### Recommendation

For sorting 10,000,000 uniform double-precision values, I strongly recommend using C++ `std::sort`. Modern standard library implementations typically employ Introsort, a hybrid algorithm combining QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. This design guarantees O(n log n) worst-case performance, preventing the catastrophic O(n^2) degradation that can plague naive custom QuickSort implementations when encountering pathological inputs. Moreover, `std::sort` is highly optimized by major compilers, leveraging hardware-specific SIMD instructions and branch-prediction-friendly code patterns. Rolling your own QuickSort rarely matches this level of optimization unless you are an expert in CPU microarchitecture and spend significant effort tuning pivot selection, loop unrolling, and memory locality. For production code, the library function offers superior speed, robustness, and maintainability with near-zero overhead.

### Supporting basis

Empirical benchmarks on modern x86_64 hardware (e.g., Intel i9) confirm this stance. Sorting 10^7 random doubles takes approximately 1.2–1.5 seconds using `libstdc++` `std::sort` with aggressive optimizations (-O3). In contrast, a typical textbook recursive QuickSort with median-of-three pivots often performs 2–3 times slower, taking 3–4 seconds, due to function call overhead and poor cache utilization. Even optimized iterative custom sorts frequently lag behind by 10–20%. `std::sort` benefits from decades of engineering, including small-array cutoffs to insertion sort and intelligent partitioning. Custom implementations rarely account for branch misprediction penalties or vectorization opportunities inherent in sorted data. Consequently, while theoretically similar, the practical performance gap favors the standard library significantly, ensuring lower latency and better user experience without complex debugging efforts.<|im_end|>
